title: False Friends Ambush
intro: Embarazada isn’t embarrassed. Actualmente isn’t actually. The words that look Spanish and betray you every time — match each one to what it really means.

A2.right: ashamed or awkward (not pregnant — that's 'embarazada' in Spanish)
A2.why: Embarrassed means red in the face. Pregnant is “pregnant”: a classic, and very public, mistake.

A2.right: a place to borrow books (not a bookshop — that's 'librería' in Spanish)
A2.why: You borrow books from a library and buy them in a bookshop.

A2.right: a floor covering (not a folder — that's 'carpeta' in Spanish)
A2.why: A carpet is on the floor. Your papers go in a folder.

A2.right: the way out (not success — 'éxito' in Spanish means success)
A2.why: Exit is the door out. Success is “success”.

A2.right: big in size (not long in time — 'largo' in Spanish means long)
A2.why: Large means big: a large ranch. Long is “long”.

A2.right: to fake something (not to expect or intend — 'pretender' in Spanish)
A2.why: Pretend means act as if: the outlaw pretended to be a priest. To intend is “intend”.

A2.right: in fact, really (not 'currently' — that's 'actualmente' in Spanish)
A2.why: Actually means in fact. Currently, “actualmente”, is “currently” or “at the moment”.

A2.right: to become aware of something (not to carry out — 'realizar' in Spanish)
A2.why: Realise means understand suddenly. To carry out a task is “carry out” or “do”.

A2.right: achieving what you wanted (not an event — 'suceso' in Spanish means incident)
A2.why: Success is a good result. An incident in the news, “suceso”, is an “incident” or “event”.

A2.right: one time (not the number eleven — 'once' in Spanish)
A2.why: Once means one time: I've been to Toledo once. Eleven is “eleven”.

A2.right: a metal pot for cooking (not bread — 'pan' in Spanish means bread)
A2.why: A paella is cooked in a pan. Bread, “pan”, is “bread”.

A2.right: the head of a town council (not older — 'mayor' in Spanish means older)
A2.why: The mayor runs the town hall. Older, “mayor”, is “older” or “elder”.

B1.right: to help (not to attend an event — 'asistir' in Spanish means to attend)
B1.why: Assist means help. To go to an event, “asistir”, is “attend”.

B1.right: kind and understanding (not fun or likeable — 'simpático' in Spanish means friendly)
B1.why: Sympathetic means kind when someone is suffering. A friendly person, “simpático”, is “nice” or “friendly”.

B1.right: practical and wise (not sensitive or emotional — 'sensible' in Spanish means sensitive)
B1.why: A sensible person makes wise choices. A sensitive person, “sensible”, is “sensitive”.

B1.right: unable to empty your bowels (not having a cold — 'constipado' in Spanish means a cold)
B1.why: Constipated is about your bowels. A head cold, “constipado”, is “a cold”: a mistake to avoid at the doctor's.

B1.right: a disagreement or quarrel (not a film's plot — 'argumento' in Spanish means plot)
B1.why: An argument is a quarrel. A film's plot, “argumento”, is the “plot”.

B1.right: your working life (not a degree course — 'carrera' in Spanish often means degree)
B1.why: A career is your working life. A university degree, “carrera”, is a “degree”.

B1.right: real, as opposed to imagined (not 'current' — 'actual' in Spanish means present-day)
B1.why: Actual means real: the actual cost. Present-day, “actual”, is “current”.

B1.right: in the end, finally (not 'possibly' — 'eventualmente' in Spanish means possibly)
B1.why: Eventually means in the end. Possibly, “eventualmente”, is “possibly” or “if necessary”.

B1.right: great unhappiness (not poverty — 'miseria' in Spanish often means poverty)
B1.why: Misery is deep unhappiness. Poverty, “miseria”, is “poverty”, and a tiny amount is “a pittance”.

B1.right: without much flavour (not soft — 'blando' in Spanish means soft)
B1.why: Bland food has little taste. Soft, “blando”, is “soft”.

B1.right: to start again after a pause (not to summarise — 'resumir' in Spanish)
B1.why: The meeting resumed after lunch. To summarise, “resumir”, is “summarise”.

B1.right: a senior university teacher (not any teacher — 'profesor' in Spanish covers school teachers too)
B1.why: In English only senior university staff are professors. Your English teacher is a “teacher”.

B2.right: a mutual concession (not a prior engagement — 'compromiso' in Spanish often means commitment)
B2.why: A compromise is a deal where both sides give a little. A commitment, “compromiso”, is a “commitment”.

B2.right: strong revulsion (not mild annoyance — 'disgusto' in Spanish can mean upset)
B2.why: Disgust is a strong feeling of revulsion. Being upset, “disgusto”, is “upset” or “annoyance”.

B2.right: to abuse sexually — a serious word (not to bother — 'molestar' in Spanish is much milder)
B2.why: Molest is a very serious word. For “molestar” say “bother” or “disturb”.

B2.right: a formal talk or class (not reading — 'lectura' in Spanish means reading)
B2.why: A lecture is a formal talk, often at university. Reading, “lectura”, is “reading”.

B2.right: cloth or textile (not a factory — 'fábrica' in Spanish means factory)
B2.why: Fabric is cloth. A factory, “fábrica”, is a “factory”: Valencia's silk was woven into fabric in factories.

B2.right: mentally healthy (not healthy in general — 'sano' in Spanish means healthy)
B2.why: Sane means mentally healthy, not mad. Generally healthy, “sano”, is “healthy”.

B2.right: the act of deceiving or lying (not disappointment — 'decepción' in Spanish means disappointment)
B2.why: Deception means tricking people. Disappointment, “decepción”, is “disappointment”.

B2.right: having good schooling (not polite — 'educado' in Spanish means well-mannered)
B2.why: Educated means well schooled. Polite, “educado”, is “polite” or “well-mannered”.

B2.right: eager and enthusiastic (not aroused — 'excitado' in Spanish usually has a sexual sense)
B2.why: Say “I'm excited about the trip” freely. “Excitado” in Spanish carries a sexual sense.

B2.right: not common, hard to find (not weird — 'raro' in Spanish means strange)
B2.why: A rare stamp is hard to find. Something weird, “raro”, is “strange” or “odd”.

B2.right: a subject to talk about (not a cliché — 'tópico' in Spanish means stereotype)
B2.why: A topic is a subject. Paella and flamenco for every Spaniard is a “cliché” or “stereotype”.

B2.right: making little noise (not motionless — 'quieto' in Spanish means still)
B2.why: A quiet room has little noise. “¡Estate quieto!” is “Keep still!”.

C1.right: in the end, finally (not 'recently' — 'últimamente' in Spanish means lately)
C1.why: Ultimately means in the end. Lately, “últimamente”, is “lately” or “recently”.

C1.right: a fixed expression (not language in general — 'idioma' in Spanish means language)
C1.why: An idiom is a fixed expression, like “bite the bullet”. A language, “idioma”, is a “language”.

C1.right: excellent, wonderful (not terrifying, despite the look of the word)
C1.why: Terrific means wonderful: a terrific meal. Terrifying means very frightening.

C1.right: polite and kind (not funny — 'gracioso' in Spanish means funny)
C1.why: Gracious means polite and generous. Funny, “gracioso”, is “funny”.

C1.right: a person injured or killed (not a coincidence — 'casualidad' in Spanish means chance)
C1.why: Casualties are people hurt or killed. A coincidence, “casualidad”, is a “coincidence” or “chance”.

C1.right: your handwritten name (not a firm or company — 'firma' in Spanish can mean company)
C1.why: A signature is your name in your own handwriting. A company, “firma”, is a “firm”.

C1.right: an expression of regret (not a defence — 'apología' in Spanish can mean a defence of something)
C1.why: An apology means saying sorry. A defence of something, “apología”, is a “defence” or “justification”.

C1.right: the natural colour of your facial skin (not your body build — 'complexión' in Spanish means build)
C1.why: Complexion is about the skin of your face: a pale complexion. Body build, “complexión”, is “build”.

C1.right: drunk (not poisoned by food — 'intoxicación' in Spanish usually means food poisoning)
C1.why: Intoxicated means drunk. Bad seafood gives you “food poisoning”.

C1.right: to avoid giving a direct answer (not to abuse public office — 'prevaricar' in Spanish)
C1.why: A politician who prevaricates dodges the question. Abusing office is “misconduct in public office”.

C1.right: great joy at a success (not retirement — 'jubilación' in Spanish means retirement)
C1.why: The town greeted the news with jubilation. Retirement, “jubilación”, is “retirement”.

C1.right: a supporter or regular customer (not a boss — 'patrón' in Spanish means boss)
C1.why: The Medici were patrons of the arts. A boss, “patrón”, is a “boss” or “employer”.
